Two tigers, two tigers, running fast, running fast

You’re my little, little apple, I can never love you enough

Jingle bells, jingle bells, jingle all the way

Come on, to the left, draw a dragon with me; on your right, paint a rainbow

As you read those four lines, did you catch yourself singing them without meaning to? (For readers who didn’t grow up in China, the other three are “Two Tigers,” the Chinese nursery version of “Frère Jacques”; “Little Apple,” the Chopstick Brothers’ 2014 smash hit; and “Wild Wolf Disco,” the viral hit of 2019.)

If you make an effort to read them normally, it can even feel like hard work. Why? Mostly, it’s the work of an earworm.

An earworm, also known as a brainworm, sticky music, stuck song syndrome or involuntary musical imagery, is a fragment of music that keeps repeating in your head, usually 15–20 seconds long.

The word comes from the German Ohrwurm. It was first borrowed into English as a loan translation by the British novelist Desmond Bagley in his 1978 novel Flyaway. [A sign of how far ahead the German-speaking world was in psychoacoustics back then? *grins*]

Put simply, an earworm is pretty much a “brainwashing” song: you never set out to learn it, yet you can always hum a few lines, and usually only those few lines. You have no idea what comes before them, or what comes after.

When the internet went mainstream at the start of the new century, music spread more easily and reached far more people. Ever since, every year has brought a few songs that sweep the whole country and play on repeat in restaurants, shops and every public square.

From Phoenix Legend’s “The Most Dazzling Ethnic Style”

to PSY’s “Gangnam Style,”

from Lady Gaga’s “Poker Face”

to Adele’s “Someone Like You.”

Just seeing a song title or a dance move right now may be enough to start the tune playing in your head.

With the rise of the mobile internet in recent years, apps built for mobile entertainment, led by Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok), have started mass-producing these hits, so much so that “Douyin hits” are replacing “brainwashing hits” as the term of choice.

From the 2018 crop, “Seaweed Dance,” “Learn to Meow,” “Desert Camel,” “Despacito” and “That Girl,”

to 2019’s “Grain in Ear,” “You Look So Good When You Smile,” “Green,” “Zombie” and “Wild Wolf Disco,” it seems as though a few songs take over the whole internet nearly every month.

The first big hit of 2020 must be this one, “Lonely Tango.”

So why are these songs so hypnotically catchy?

Kelly Jakubowski’s team at Goldsmiths, University of London [1] studied nearly 200 earworm tunes. Among the many features of the songs themselves, they found three that determine how catchy a tune is: an upbeat tempo, a simple melodic contour and some unusual intervals. The first two keep the tune simple enough for the brain to remember easily. The third keeps the simple melody sounding distinctive.

Besides those three features of the song itself, catchiness also correlates positively with exposure: a song you have heard six times is more likely to become an earworm than one you have heard only twice [2]. Douyin’s short videos usually loop endlessly, which greatly increases exposure to whatever is playing. That may be one reason Douyin is so good at producing hits.

Usually, a catchy tune that keeps popping into your head has no particular effect on your life. Or, as some people report, it can even help: humming a tune while doing the housework seems to make the work go faster.

In some situations, though, earworms can do harm. Students sitting an important exam, for instance, can be distracted by earworms that pop up uncontrollably, and their answers suffer.

Writers hammering away at their keyboards late at night before a deadline can also have their train of thought broken by earworms, and their output suffers. Er Mu, typing this very paragraph, is being plagued by “Is it the dragon on the left or the rainbow on the right?”, having recently been roped into rehearsing a dance to “Wild Wolf Disco” for the company’s annual party…

So what can we do to drive these annoying earworms away?

For this kind of uncontrollable mental activity, psychologists may have some answers.

Psychology has a famous problem called “Don’t think of a white bear,” also known as the white bear effect. Tell people not to picture a white polar bear and the result is usually the opposite: a white polar bear pops into their heads, because checking whether they are thinking about a white polar bear makes them think about it. [Want to give it a try?]

The psychologists’ solution to the white bear problem is to go and do or think about something else, rather than trying to think or not think about the bear. The same goes for earworms: think of a different tune to break the current loop. The risk, of course, is that you just drive out the old worm with a new one.

Another fix for an earworm is to sing the whole song through to the end, because one of the main reasons for the endless loop is that we don’t know where the song ends. Mozart was often teased by children practicing the piano downstairs, who would deliberately play an incomplete scale. Their unfinished do re mi drove poor Mozart up the wall, and he would rush downstairs to finish it off with fa sol la ti.

So if a snatch of some catchy song keeps playing in your head until it interferes with work or study, try learning the whole song, melody and lyrics. When it suddenly pops into your head, keep singing until you reach the end.

Will somebody please tell me what the next line is?!

We still don’t fully understand how earworms arise. A BBC program once remarked that we know less about our planet’s oceans, and the deep sea in particular, than about the vast skies above our heads. And isn’t the same true of the brain sitting right on top of our necks? There is still so much waiting to be explored. Getting to the bottom of earworms will take a great deal more work from researchers in many fields: acousticians, brain scientists, neuroscientists, biologists and others. I hope this article draws some attention to the question and gets people talking about it.

Finally, have you ever been plagued by an earworm, or had some similar experience? We’d love to hear about it.

In a few days comes the most important day of the year for Chinese people, the Lunar New Year. You may be on your way home for the family reunion right now, or still holding the fort at work. Er Mu and Ziyu wish you, a little early:

A lucky Year of the Rat!

Good health!

Smooth sailing at work (and in your studies)!

Abundance year after year!

Main references:

1. Jakubowski, Kelly; Finkel, Sebastian; Stewart, Lauren; Müllensiefen, Daniel (2017). “Dissecting an earworm: Melodic features and song popularity predict involuntary musical imagery.” Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts. American Psychological Association (APA). 11 (2): 122–135.

2. Byron, T. P., & Fowles, L. C. (2013). Repetition and recency increases involuntary musical imagery of previously unfamiliar songs. Psychology of Music, 43, 375–389.
